questions.problem: The function ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation $x{y}^{″}-(x+1){y}^{′}+y=0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x)\cdot {e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x({u}^{″}{e}^{x}+2{u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})-(x+1)({u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x})+u{e}^{x} & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux)-{e}^{x}{u}^{′}(x+1)-{e}^{x}u(x+1)+{e}^{x}u & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+2{u}^{′}x+ux-{u}^{′}(x+1)-u(x+1)+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(2x-x-1)+u(x-x-1+1)) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0,$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}x+{u}^{′}(x-1)=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}x+w(x-1)=0.
$$

This is a separable equation that has the solution

$$
w={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}x{e}^{-x}\,⟹\,u=-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}(-{c}_{1}(1+x){e}^{-x}+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=-1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)=(1+x).
$$

questions.problem: Given the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,{e}^{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,-1,{e}^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{2x}-{y}^{2}z)\text{ }k \\  & =2{e}^{2x}\text{ }i-2yz\text{ }j-{y}^{2}k \\ ∇\,f(1,-1,{e}^{2}) & =2{e}^{2}\text{ }i-2(-1)({e}^{2})\text{ }j-(-1)^{2}k \\  & =2{e}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{2}\,j-k \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,-1,{e}^{2})\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2{e}^{2},2{e}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y+1,\,z-{e}^{2}⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,-8,-1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $2x+y-2z=-7.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z & =-7 \\ 2(1)+(-3)+7 & =2z \\ 6 & =2z \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-3,3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-3,3⟩-⟨-2,-8,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,5,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot 2+5\cdot 1+4\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|6+5-8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|\,3\,|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v(u-1)^{2} \\ v{u}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=v(u-1)^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=v{u}^{2}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2(u-1)v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =(u-1)^{2} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2uv & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & ={u}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2(u-1)v & (u-1)^{2} \\ 2uv & {u}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(u-1)v\cdot {u}^{2}-(u-1)^{2}\cdot 2uv \\  & =2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ 2{u}^{2}(u-1)v-2u(u-1)^{2}v & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v(u-(u-1)) & =0 \\ 2u(u-1)v & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $2u(u-1)v=0$ defines the lines $u=0,$ $u=1,$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane.

questions.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{23}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-4,{u}_{23}=3,$ and ${l}_{21}\cdot {u}_{23}=-12.$
